xref.title: Nash the Slash (Jeff Plunman, Toronto, 1948–2014) – Surgical Bandages Adopted After Three Mile Island Accident (1979); David Gilmour Offered Guitar Part but Nash Refused All Guitars
xref.body: Nash the Slash's real name was Jeff Plunman, born in Toronto on March 26, 1948. The stage name came from a character in a 1927 Laurel and Hardy silent film. He co-founded the prog band FM in 1975 and audiences could see his face briefly, but after the nuclear accident at Three Mile Island near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania in March 1979, Nash adopted surgical bandages that completely obscured his face as a way of raising awareness about what could happen if a nuclear plant melted down. He left FM around 1980 to resume his solo career, toured with Gary Numan and the Tubes, hung out with Iggy Pop and Daniel Lanois, and Brian Eno collaborated on his records. David Gilmour of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs — but Nash refused because he never used guitars on any of his songs. He made records until 2012, was especially popular in Germany and Poland, and died of an apparent heart attack at his Toronto home on May 10, 2014, at age 66. His music and costumes are managed by the Nash the Slash Legacy organization and much was donated to the National Music Center in Calgary. His best-known record was 1984's American Bandages. "David Gilmore of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs, but Nash refused because he never, ever used guitars on any of his songs."

xref.title: Early Label Rejection & Sire Signing (1975)
xref.body: The Ramones were signed by Seymour Stein to Sire Records in 1975 after he discovered them in a Manhattan bar. Other labels refused to sign them because they were considered "too weird," played "too fast," were "too amateurish," and "too funny looking." Mainstream rock radio also rejected them, seeing them as a joke. "back then, nobody wanted to touch the Ramones. They were just too weird. They played too fast. They were too amateurish. And they were too funny looking for all the other labels."

xref.title: Acral Lentiginous Melanoma Diagnosis and Refusal of Amputation (July 1977)
xref.body: In July 1977, a doctor in London diagnosed Bob Marley with acral lentiginous melanoma, a rare form of skin cancer discovered under his toenail that was not well documented in medical texts at the time. Despite the doctors' advice for toe amputation, Marley refused, citing his Rastafarian belief that removing any body part would be a sin, opting instead for a skin graft from his thigh performed by a Miami specialist. "In July, he visited a doctor in London, and they discovered he had something called Acro-leteginus melanoma, a pre-existing form of skin cancer under the nail that at the time wasn't well covered in the medical textbooks." "But Bob refused, saying that as a rastifarian, it would be a sin to have any body part removed."

xref.title: Paul Simonon's Bass Trashing Incident (1979)
xref.body: During a show at the Palladium in New York on September 21, 1979, bassist Paul Simonon smashed his instrument on stage. His frustration stemmed from the crowd's perceived lack of engagement, which he attributed to bouncers preventing the audience from standing up. The incident occurred around 10:43 pm, as evidenced by his broken wristwatch. This moment was captured in an iconic, out-of-focus photograph by Penny Smith, which later became the cover of "London Calling." "Simmon was in a very bad mood that night at the palladium in New York. He was upset that the crowd just wasn't into the gig, largely because the bouncers had refused to let the audience stand up and get into the show."

xref.title: Inspiration from The Mansion – Blood Sugar Sex Magik Recording (1991)
xref.body: During the recording of "Blood Sugar Sex Magik" in a historic mansion, John Frusciante embraced the isolated and reputedly haunted environment. Unlike Chad Smith, who refused to stay there, Frusciante loved the house and found it inspirational, ready to disconnect from the outside world. He believed friendly ghosts resided there and even mused that the spirit of a person who died in the house might have influenced his guitar sound. "There are definitely ghosts in this house, said John, but they are very friendly."

xref.title: Rain's Transformation into Oasis (1991)
xref.body: In 1991, after a gig by Liam Gallagher's band Rain, Liam and his bandmates asked Noel Gallagher to manage them. Noel refused to manage but offered to join as lead guitarist, stating his original songs were far superior to Rain's material, leading to the band accepting him and transforming into Oasis. xref.title: First Departure from Red Hot Chili Peppers (May 7, 1992)
xref.body: After escalating tensions, interviews he hated, and feeling reduced to a "performing monkey," John Frusciante refused to go on stage at Sonic City in Japan on May 7, 1992, just minutes before a show was to begin. He declared, "I quit," citing an inability to do justice to his creations and hearing voices telling him to leave. Although he reluctantly played that final, poor-quality 15-song set, it marked his last show with the Chili Peppers for six years. The band explained his departure as an inability to cope with mental stress. "I've reached the stage where I cannot do justice to what I've created. I can't give you what it takes to be in this band anymore."

xref.title: Lollapalooza "Party in a Bottle" Incident (1992)
xref.body: Backstage at Lollapalooza in 1992, Al Jourgensen forced someone to drink from a bottle of Bushmills whiskey with a broken, jagged neck, threatening physical harm if they refused. It was later revealed that Jourgensen was known to add a "dollop of acid" to his Bushmills, creating what he referred to as a "party in a bottle," though this particular addition fortunately did not occur that day. "I ended up backstage with Al at Lala Paloza in 1992 and he made me drink from a bottle of bush mill whiskey that had dropped on the pavement."

xref.title: Encounter with Duff McKagan and Death (1994)
xref.body: After escaping rehab, Kurt Cobain took Delta Flight 788 to Seattle and coincidentally sat next to Guns N' Roses bassist Duff McKagan, also a veteran of rehab. Cobain refused a ride from McKagan upon landing, signed autographs, and disappeared. He then acquired drugs, returned to the room above the greenhouse at his and Courtney Love's Lake Washington Boulevard home, got high, and died by suicide, believed to be on April 5th, 1994. The news of his death broke on Friday, April 8th. "Soon, he was on Delta Flight 788 to Seattle, and by sheer coincidence, he was sitting next to Guns & Roses bass player Duff McAgan, himself, a junkie we have veteran."

xref.title: Ticketmaster Legal Challenge (1994)
xref.body: Pearl Jam launched a legal action against Ticketmaster in 1994, aiming to tour with tickets priced below $20 and a service charge no more than $1.80. Ticketmaster refused, stating they needed to charge at least $2 to cover costs. Despite a significant fight, testimony before the U.S. Congress, and an attempt to circumvent Ticketmaster's network, the case accusing Ticketmaster of being anti-competitive collapsed in 1995. The band now uses Ticketmaster for their ticketing. "Despite a good fight, testimony before the U.S. Congress and an attempt to circumvent Ticketmaster's ticket selling network, it didn't work."

xref.title: Russian Customs Incident (1999)
xref.body: On February 4, 1999, Garbage faced problems with Russian customs agents when attempting to cross the border to perform in Tallinn, Estonia. Their road cases were stenciled with the band's name, "Garbage," which Russian customs officials interpreted literally as a declaration of "trash" for export. Despite the band's repeated explanations that it was their name, the agents refused to clear them, leading to the cancellation of their show in Tallinn. "The kids in Tallinn, Estonia did not get their garbage show that night."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Evolution of Public Image (1990s-2001)
xref.body: In the mid-to-late 1990s, their live performances initially featured no costumes, just them and a DJ booth. They later experimented with black bags over their heads and Halloween masks, began objecting to photos and filming, and refused to speak if filmed, with the robot helmets and matching gloves first appearing in 2001. "When they performed live in the middle in late 1990s, there were no costumes, just them and a DJ booth. Then they started playing with their image. Sometimes they'd appear with black bags over their heads. Other times they brought out Halloween masks. They started to object to photographs and filming. And if they were to be filmed, they wouldn't speak. The robot helmets first started appearing in 2001 and came with matching gloves."

xref.title: Final Visit from Mike Starr (April 4, 2002)
xref.body: On Thursday, April 4, 2002, former bandmate Mike Starr visited Lane Staley's condo and was shocked by his emaciated appearance, offering to call 911. Staley vehemently refused, stating he would never speak to Starr again if he did. Starr left feeling angry and discouraged, with Staley pleading, "not like this, don't leave like this." Mike Starr is believed to have been the last person to see Lane Staley alive. "Mike was shocked at how bad Lane looked, an offer to call 911. Lane said, if you do that, I will never talk to you again."

xref.title: Layne Staley's Last Known Interaction (April 4, 2002)
xref.body: On Thursday, April 4, 2002, former Alice in Chains bandmate Mike Starr visited Layne Staley's condo. Starr was shocked by Staley's severely deteriorated appearance and urged him to call 911, but Staley refused. Starr eventually left, feeling angry, discouraged, and sad, telling Staley, "not like this, don't leave like this." Mike Starr is believed to have been the last person to see Layne Staley alive. "Looks like he was the last guy to see Lane alive."

xref.title: Heathrow Arrest (2003)
xref.body: On February 3, 2003, Courtney Love was arrested at Heathrow Airport after being accused of abusing the cabin crew on Virgin Atlantic Flight 8 from Los Angeles to London. The alleged problem arose when the crew reportedly refused to allow her nurse into the first-class section where Love was seated, prompting the captain to radio ahead for police awaiting her on the tarmac. "The problem stemmed, allegedly, from the crew refusing to allow her nurse into where she was sitting in the first class section."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Magic Stick Assault (December 13, 2003) – Jack White Beat Von Bondies Singer Jason Stollsteimer
xref.body: On a Saturday night at the Magic Stick club in Detroit during the CD release party for a local band called Blanche, Jack White approached Von Bondies singer Jason Stollsteimer, spat in his face, and began punching him. When Stollsteimer fell to the floor, White continued hitting him until bystanders pulled him away. White filed a counter-complaint claiming self-defense. He initially pleaded not guilty, then changed his plea to guilty of misdemeanor assault and battery on March 9, 2004. Sentence: $500 fine, $200 court costs, one year of anger management. White maintained that Stollsteimer had grabbed him and pulled out his hair, and that his retaliation lasted less than 10 seconds. He also alleged that Stollsteimer refused to wash off the blood before posing for press photos sent to NME the next morning, and that the permanently damaged eye he claimed was a pre-existing injury from a contact lens incident as a teenager. White and Stollsteimer had not spoken for two years prior to the incident. "The entire event was completely exploited by him, his band and his managers and legal professionals."

xref.title: Tom Delonge's Second Departure (2014-2015)
xref.body: Tom Delonge quit the band again around 2014, although he briefly returned proposing group therapy led by motivational speaker Tony Robbins, which did not resolve underlying issues. Communication ceased once more, leading to indefinite delays for a planned 2013 album. His manager eventually sent an email, one week before a scheduled studio session, stating Tom's indefinite unwillingness to participate in Blink-182 activities. The band issued a statement announcing his departure, to which Tom countered that the band demanded he put all other projects on hold for an album and tour within six months. He refused these terms and officially left. "Tom's manager sent an email... saying that Tom did not want to participate in any Blink activities indefinitely."

xref.title: Death at MGM Grand (March 3, 2017)
xref.body: Chris Cornell died by hanging himself in room 1136 of the MGM Grand in Detroit on March 3, 2017, after performing a gig at the Fox Theatre. After the show, he returned to the hotel with his bodyguard, Martin Christen, and was experiencing anxiety. He had taken some Ativan tablets and later told his wife, Vicki, in a phone call around 11:35 pm, that he had taken an "extra Ativan or two," slurring his words and sounding groggy. Vicki called Martin around 12:15 am, asking him to check on Chris. Martin found the room locked, and after hotel security refused assistance, he kicked in the door. He then kicked in the locked bathroom door, finding Chris on the floor with an exercise band around his neck and blood from his mouth. Paramedics were called at 12:56 am, CPR was performed, but he was pronounced dead at 1:30 am. "Chris Cornell, who died on March 3, 2017 in room 11.36 of the MGM Grand Hotel in Detroit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Discovery of Death (2017)
xref.body: Concerned by Chris's abrupt hang-up, Vicki called Martin Kirsten, who returned to room 1136 around 12:15 AM, approximately 40 minutes after his last departure. Despite having a key, the door was latched from the inside. Security refused to open it without authorization, so Kirsten kicked the door open. After searching the room and finding the bathroom door locked, he kicked that open as well. Inside, Cornell was found on the floor with blood around his mouth and a red exercise band around his neck, which was attached to a carabiner tightly jammed into the doorframe. Paramedics arrived just before 1 AM, but it was too late. Chris was pronounced dead at 1:30 AM, with police ruling it a suicide by hanging. "Inside, Cornell was found laying on the floor, blood running down his mouth and a red exercise band around his neck. The band had been attached to a carbonyl, which is a type of shackle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Death (July 26, 2023) – Found Unresponsive in London Apartment; Coroner Ruled Natural Causes in January 2024
xref.body: Sinéad O'Connor led a troubled life with both physical and mental health struggles from the beginning. During her career she became an icon for refusing to bend to anyone or anything, always doing everything her own way. She survived multiple suicide attempts over the years, and friends and followers were regularly concerned about her well-being. She was found unresponsive in her London apartment on July 26, 2023, and was declared dead at the scene. In January 2024, the Coroner's report determined she died of natural causes — nothing suspicious, case closed. Her first two albums are considered stone-cold classics. "She became an icon as someone who refused to bend and insisted on doing everything and I mean everything her way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Mother's Milk" Nudity Lawsuit
xref.body: The cover of *Mother's Milk* sparked controversy due to its depiction of Don Lane, a topless woman cradling the band members. Lane claimed the band did not ask for her permission to use her image. Several record store chains, including Walmart, refused to stock or display the record due to perceived female nudity, despite the minimal exposure. Walmart specifically opted for a censored version where band members were enlarged to cover more of Lane. Compounding the issue, limited promotional posters were distributed with Lane's breasts completely exposed, again without her knowledge. Lane subsequently sued the band and was awarded a $50,000 settlement. "She sued the band and won a settlement of $50,000."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 1

xref.title: Advance and Copyright Deadlock with EMI
xref.body: Radiohead, after having sold 25 million records and delivered tens of millions in revenue to EMI since 1992, requested an advance of £10 million for a new contract, but EMI would not offer more than £3 million. Crucially, EMI also refused to grant Radiohead any control over their back catalog's copyright, insisting on retaining rights for the standard 50 years, leading to an insurmountable deadlock. "Radiohead also wanted some measure of control over their back catalog and how that music would be exploited going forward. But EMI would not budge."

xref.title: Backlash, Threats, and Sponsor Withdrawals
xref.body: When news of the coming-out episode spread, hate mail flooded Ellen's offices. Televangelists Revolgary Fallwell and Pat Robertson publicly mocked her as "Ellen DeGenerate" and joined others in signing a letter condemning the show for promoting homosexuality. A bomb threat was even called into the studio. An ABC affiliate in Birmingham, Alabama, refused to air the episode. Fearing controversy, major sponsors including Chrysler, General Motors, Johnson & Johnson, JC Penny, Domino's Pizza, and McDonald's withdrew their advertising. The Human Rights Campaign and a cruise line targeting lesbian clientele attempted to buy these advertising spots, but ABC declined their ads. "Revolgary fall well and televanjalous Pat Robertson publicly mock DeGeneres as Ellen DeGenerate and joined others in signing a letter that decried the show as a blatant attempt to promote homosexuality."

xref.title: Band's Stand Against Label Interference
xref.body: In an unusual move for a new band, Linkin Park directly met with Warner Brothers executives and firmly rejected various label suggestions, including demands to remove rapping, change Mike Shinoda's rap style to mimic Fred Durst, bring in a reggae vocalist named Matt Lyons, or introduce gimmicks for DJ Joe Hahn like wearing a cowboy hat and lab coat. They also refused to change their logo, which some at the label found "too Asian." "And the meeting was risky because new bands just don't show up in the boardrooms of major record labels and start dictating terms for how they were to be marketed and how their fan club should be treated."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: British Shoegaze Band
xref.body: Engineers were a British band that had been working with shoegaze sounds since at least 2003, predating the 2010s "semi-revival" of the genre. Their continued presence highlighted the dedication of adherents who refused to give up on the sound. "Well, there were engineers, a British band who had been working with these sounds since at least 2003."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

xref.title: Columbia Records Dispute Over Name
xref.body: In 1975, Columbia Records expressed interest in the band and paid for the recording of seven songs, but demanded they change their name from "Death" due to concerns about commercial viability. When the band refused, Columbia withdrew its offer, claiming a group with that name would have "zero commercial success." "In 1975, Columbia Records expressed interest in the band and paid for the recording of seven songs. And while the music was good, the label did not like the band's name and demanded that they find something else. When death refused, Columbia bailed, saying that a group with that name would have zero commercial success."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

xref.title: Contribution to Screamo Evolution
xref.body: The Refused were among the groups that played a role in the development and evolution of Screamo, a subgenre characterized by its darker, louder, and more intense sound. "Groups like the used, the refused...all contributed to the evolution of Screamo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Cultural Icon of Political Punk
xref.body: The Clash, particularly through Joe Strummer, were regarded as the quintessential political and activist punk band, embodying a defiant spirit that resonated with millions worldwide and refused to compromise. "He was the political punk, the activist punk, the punk that refused to bend. For millions around the world, he was the guy who embodied the best of the punk spirit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 8: (30-21)

xref.title: Declined to Perform for Donald Trump
xref.body: Celine Dion was one of the artists who refused invitations to perform for Donald Trump on multiple occasions. "The killers, Celine Dion, Meat Lough and Erasmith all turned him down to play various things."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Def Jam Royalty Dispute
xref.body: Following the "Licensed to Ill" tour, Def Jam records demanded a new album immediately, which the Beastie Boys, feeling "burned out," refused. In response, Def Jam began withholding royalties that rightfully belonged to the band, leading to a legal dispute that lasted for months before the Beastie Boys broke free. "So Def Jam started holding back royalties, money that should have rightfully gone to the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Discovery of Death by Bodyguard
xref.body: At 12:15 AM, Martin Kirsten went to Chris Cornell's locked hotel room door and, after security refused entry, kicked it in. He found the bathroom door also locked and kicked that in as well, discovering Cornell on the floor with a red exercise band around his neck and blood coming from his mouth, not breathing. A hotel medic and ambulance arrived shortly after, but at 1:30 AM, Chris Cornell was declared dead. "He kicked that door in, too, and found Chris on the floor with a red exercise band around his neck and blood running from his mouth."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Dispute Over Ticket Price Split
xref.body: Pearl Jam sought an "all-in" ticket price of $25 but wanted Ticketmaster to reduce its service charge from $4 to $2, which would increase the band's take from $21 to $23 per ticket. Ticketmaster refused this demand, instead suggesting that Pearl Jam could achieve their $25 ticket price if they agreed to accept less for the base price of the ticket. "But then Pearl Jam said, no, no, no, no, you charge $2 so we could make $23 for ticket and ticket master would refuse saying that the band could have their $25 ticket if they agreed to take less."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 2

xref.title: Early Image and Influence on Lad Culture
xref.body: Around 1985, Happy Mondays' casual image, characterized by wearing trainers and "regular" shirts, was questioned by record labels seeking a defined look. The band refused to change, and this style, which they had cultivated for years, later became a foundational element of "lad culture" that emerged approximately a decade later. "And they came up and they were like, what's your image? And we was like, well, this is how we dress. And they were like, well, what you wear in trainers and getting images like, you know, we're not wearing, you know, this is how we dress."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Failed Song Licensing for "Blue Velvet"
xref.body: For his 1986 film "Blue Velvet," Lynch attempted to license "Song to the Siren" by This Mortal Coil from 4AD, but the label refused. This led him to collaborate with Angelo Badalamenti and Julee Cruise for the film's soundtrack.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Family's Unsuccessful Attempts to Help
xref.body: Despite his mother and other family members attempting to maintain contact and encourage rehab, Lane Staley withdrew further, refusing to answer calls or the door, believing that since 13 previous rehab attempts had failed, further efforts would be futile. "If anyone did reach him and suggested more rehab, he refused. It had already been 13 times, and nothing worked, so why bother?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Fatal Car-Jacking Attempt
xref.body: Rhett Forrester, the singer for the New York metal band Riot in the early 1980s, and later a member of groups like the Calgary-based The Black Symphony, was murdered on September 22, 1996. He was shot and killed during an attempted car-jacking while stopped at a traffic light in Tucker, Georgia, after refusing to give up his car. A confession to the crime emerged years later. "When he refused to give up his car, he was shot and killed. It took years before someone confessed to the crime."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Feud with Guns N' Roses
xref.body: The bad blood between Nirvana and Guns N' Roses, particularly with Axl Rose, started when Kurt Cobain refused an offer for Nirvana to open for Guns N' Roses on a major world tour. Kurt viewed Guns N' Roses as "too big" and was concerned that aligning with them would be perceived as selling out, stating Nirvana was not a "typical Guns n' Roses type of band that has absolutely nothing to say." Axl Rose, who was a fan of Nirvana (even wearing a Nirvana hat in the "Don't Cry" video), felt snubbed and began publicly insulting Kurt and Courtney Love as "junkies," claiming their daughter had birth defects due to their drug use. "It began when Kurt refused an offer by the Gunners to have Nirvana open for them on one of their massive world tours."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Feud with Nirvana
xref.body: The animosity began when Nirvana refused an offer to open for Guns N' Roses on a major world tour, a decision Kurt Cobain made due to concerns about being perceived as "sellouts" and his disdain for what he called the "typical Guns n' Roses type of band that has absolutely nothing to say." Axl Rose, a fan of Nirvana who even wore a Nirvana hat in the "Don't Cry" video, felt insulted and began publicly calling Kurt and Courtney Love "junkies," claiming their daughter had birth defects due to their drug use. "It began when Kurt refused an offer by the Gunners to have Nirvana open for them on one of their massive world tours."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Focus on Family and Continued Secrecy
xref.body: Harriet and David, who had been married for years, decided to prioritize spending time with their children. Although they reportedly continue to make music, they are too "paranoid" to release anything. An intense fan once located their home address, but the couple refused to speak to them, and the other two band members also declined interviews. "Harriet and David, who've been married for years, decided that they needed to spend more time with their kids. According to people who know them, they continue to make music but are too paranoid to release anything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Initial Openness and Later Withdrawal on Epilepsy
xref.body: Initially, Ian Curtis was very proactive about his epilepsy, joining the British Epilepsy Association and openly discussing his condition. However, he soon ceased being open, eventually refusing to talk about it altogether. "At first, Ian was very proactive, joining the British Epilepsy Association and was willing to talk to anybody about what he faced. But he soon stopped being so open about his condition and eventually refused to talk about it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Lydon's Refusal to Write Lyrics (1990s)
xref.body: During a 1990s reunion, three-quarters of the Sex Pistols recorded music for a potential second album with producer Chris Thomas. They presented these tracks on cassette to Johnny Lydon for him to write lyrics. Lydon refused, stating he was "miffed that he wasn't involved in the writing and the recording of the music," which effectively halted the project. "They then put everything on cassette and then slipped it under the door of Johnny Lydon's room and told him to write some lyrics. Mifft that he wasn't involved in the writing and the recording of the music, he refused, or so he says, and that killed the project in its tracks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Reaction to Joey's Illness and Death
xref.body: Johnny Ramone reportedly refused to visit or call Joey while he was dying in the hospital and did not attend his funeral, reflecting the deep personal tensions between them. "There were stories that when Joey lay dying in the hospital, Johnny refused to visit or call."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Last Call with Bob Geldof
xref.body: Between 4 AM and 5 AM on the day of his death, he made two calls to Bob Geldof, engaging in a loud, 20-minute argument. He attempted to persuade Geldof to lift an injunction against Paula Yates, allowing the children to come to Australia for Christmas, but Geldof refused. Hutchence was heard screaming phrases like, "your children hate you. I'm their father, little man." "Hutchins called Bob Geldoff twice. Michael wanted to persuade Bob to drop the cordon junction against Paula and let the three kids come to Australia for Christmas."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Live Performance Absence
xref.body: After an initial tour, Kate Bush refused to play any live shows for 35 years, which contributed to an aura of mystery, myth, and legend around her. This sustained enigma, combined with her unique artistry, has resulted in one of the most loyal and fanatical fan bases in the world. "And because she refused to play any live shows for 35 years after one initial tour, she was surrounded by an aura of mystery and myth and legend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Long Hiatus from Live Performances
xref.body: After an initial tour, Kate Bush famously refrained from playing any live shows for 35 years. This decision contributed to an aura of mystery, myth, and legend surrounding her, captivating many and fostering one of the most loyal and fanatical fan bases globally. "because she refused to play any live shows for 35 years after one initial tour, she was surrounded by an aura of mystery and myth and legend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mainstream Radio Blackout
xref.body: In 1978, mainstream radio stations in America refused to play Ramones records, deeming punk rock "too dangerous, too weird, too violent, too polarizing, too class conscious, too political." The American music industry largely considered punk a fad to be ignored until it disappeared. "Mainstream radio stations wouldn't touch punk rock. Too dangerous, too weird, too violent, too polarizing, too class conscious, too political."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: McLaren's Attempted Re-hiring of Matlock
xref.body: Two weeks after Matlock's departure, Malcolm McLaren called him, acknowledging that his replacement, Sid Vicious, was not working out and asked Matlock to rejoin the band. Matlock refused, stating it was "too late" and he wanted "none of you locked anymore." "What if Madlock had returned to the Sex Pistols? How would their future and their legend and myth and legacy turned out?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Michael Stipe's Dislike for "Superman"
xref.body: Michael Stipe found the song "Superman" to be "boring" and refused to sing lead on it. He was outvoted by the rest of the band, leading to Mike Mills taking over lead vocal duties for the track, with Stipe providing backup vocals. "Everybody in the band really liked it except Michael Steip Boring he said But Steip was outvoted and the song was recorded for the band's 1986 album Life's Rich Pageant"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Origin of Brother/Sister Myth
xref.body: The idea that Jack and Meg White were brother and sister started as a joke they perpetuated when The White Stripes first began. When they became famous, the truth about their ex-husband and wife relationship was "outed," but some fans continued to believe the original story. "Actually as a joke, when the white stripes started both Jack and Meg insisted that they were brother and sister. But when they got famous, the truth was outed, yet some people refused to believe it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: Mob 47 is highlighted as a band from Sweden's hardcore scene, indicating the genre's international reach beyond North America. "There was Sweden with Mob 47, the refused in a few others."

xref.title: Paul "Guigsy" McGuigan's Departure (Around Fourth Album)
xref.body: Bass player Paul "Guigsy" McGuigan resigned around the same time as Bonehead, doing so via fax and refusing to take calls from Noel or Liam. This departure is also speculated to be a preemptive move to avoid being fired. "Same thing with bass player Paul Giggsie McGwiggan. He left around the same time as Bonehead, except that he resigned by facts and then refused to take any calls from Noll or Liam."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Death Lawsuits – Seven Demo Vocal Tracks, Royalties, Tribute Concert Proceeds
xref.body: After Cornell's death, Vicki Cornell filed suits over two primary issues: the rights to seven vocal demo tracks recorded in early 2017 on his laptop, apparently destined for a new Soundgarden album, and the disbursement of Soundgarden royalties. Soundgarden counter-sued, alleging Vicki misappropriated proceeds from a 2019 tribute concert. Both sides went to war over social media rights and Chris's posthumous participation in any band activities. Vicki's offer of $4 million per remaining member, then $7 million, was refused. A settlement was announced on April 17, 2023: the seven songs will be finished and released. "This dispute has never been about money or the band. This is their life's work and their legacy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Refusal of Electra Deal
xref.body: Daniel Johnston famously refused a major record deal from Electra, explaining his decision by stating that Metallica, who were signed to Electra, were "obviously possessed by Satan." He also fired his manager who brought the deal, believing the manager was "obviously possessed too," demonstrating his unique worldview impacting his career choices. "Electra came calling with a major deal, but Daniel refused to sign. Why? Well, because Metallica was on Electra and they were obviously possessed by Satan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Refusal of Wider Release for "Pocket Watch"
xref.body: Despite bootlegs appearing from places like Italy, Dave Grohl refused Jenny Toomey's requests to officially release "Pocket Watch" on vinyl or CD. He stated a preference to keep it exclusively as a cassette-only album, limiting its official distribution. "When bootlegs started appearing from places like Italy, she begged Dave to allow her to release the album on vinyl, or on CD, but Dave said, no, no, no, I would just rather keep it as a cassette thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Refusal to Conduct Recordings
xref.body: For many years, John Philip Sousa proudly refused to conduct any orchestras in recording situations. He famously stated, "I have never been in the Gramophone company's office in my life," demonstrating his steadfast opposition to the recording industry until his death in 1932. "And for years, Susa refused to conduct any orchestras in any recording situations, proudly saying that I have never been in the Gramophone company's office in my life."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music vs Technology Over The Years

xref.title: Refusal to License Song
xref.body: The band famously declined numerous lucrative offers to license "The Future's So Bright, I Gotta Wear Shades" for commercial use, prioritizing the song's intended grim message over financial gain. "And despite offers of up to a million dollars to license the song by everyone from Ford and Bauch and Lomb and AT&T, Ray Bann sunglasses and even the US Army, they have refused any and all offers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 50 Biggest All-Time Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders: Part 1

xref.title: Refusal to Make Videos (After Initial Singles)
xref.body: After dutifully creating music videos for the first four singles from their debut album *Ten*, Pearl Jam refused to make any more for about six years. This resistance was a significant statement during an era when music videos were considered essential for promotion, reflecting the alt-rock ethos that often expressed disdain for the "We Must Make a Video" practice. "Pearl Jam refused to do any more for about six years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 2

xref.title: Refusal to Play Encores
xref.body: Elvis Presley famously refused to perform encores. This policy led to the iconic "Elvis has left the building" announcement, which was specifically designed to prompt fans, who often desired more music, to leave the venue. "Elvis Presley refused to do Encore's. Hence the famous Elvis has left the building announcement, designed to clear out fans who wanted more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Refusal to Use Songs in Commercials
xref.body: At one point, when they were a punk band, the Beastie Boys refused to let their songs be used in commercials. "were once a punk band refused to let their songs be used in commercials."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Relationship Obfuscation (Brother and Sister Pretense)
xref.body: Jack and Meg White deliberately obscured their true relationship, often pretending to be brother and sister to the public. This charade was maintained to "throw everybody off" and they notably refused to be interviewed separately. "At first, they pretended to be brother and sister just to throw everybody off. They refused to be interviewed separately."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Relationship of Jack and Meg White
xref.body: Contrary to a widely circulated myth, Jack (John Anthony Gillis) and Meg White are not brother and sister; they are ex-husband and wife. They met in Detroit in 1994, where Meghan Martha White was a bartender at Memphis Smoke, and John Anthony Gillis was an ex-furniture upholsterer. They married on September 12, 1996, with Jack taking Meg's last name in a reversal of tradition. They started their band, released albums, and then divorced on March 24, 2000, but remained friends and bandmates. The "brother and sister" claim began as a joke when the band started, and despite the truth being revealed when they gained fame, some people still refused to believe it. "For once and for all, they are not brother and sister. They are actually ex-husband and wife. John Anthony Gillis met Meghan Martha White in Detroit in 1994. She was a bartender at a place called Memphis Smoke, and he was an ex-furniture upholsterer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Resilience in Attawapiskat
xref.body: Despite Attawapiskat being in the news for serious issues like housing crises, a major suicide epidemic, and drug problems, Adrian Sutherland and others like him refuse to give up on their home and neighbors, highlighting a spirit of resilience. "From Anna Wapisgad in Northern Ontario, a place that's been in the news for so many sad reasons like housing crisis, a major suicide epidemic, drug problems and more. But guys like Adrian Sutherland refused to give up on their home and their neighbors."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Retailer Blacklist of In Utero
xref.body: Walmart and Kmart, significant record retailers at the time, refused to stock *In Utero* because it "didn't conform with their family values." "Then again, Walmart and Kmart, two department stores, which were also important record retailers back then, refused to stock the album because it didn't conform with their family values."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rivers Cuomo's Initial Rejection of "Buddy Holly"
xref.body: Rivers Cuomo initially refused to consider including "Buddy Holly" on Weezer's debut album, deeming it "too cheesy" and an outlier compared to his other compositions. He felt it didn't fit the band's intended sound. "For the longest time, he refused to consider including the song and Weezer's debut album because it was too cheesy."

xref.title: Seinfeld Reunion on Curb Your Enthusiasm
xref.body: David had previously refused to do a Seinfeld reunion, but he found it funny to integrate one into *Curb Your Enthusiasm*, seeing it as the "perfect way to do it, but not really do it." The entire season revolved around a fictionalized reboot of the original series, utilizing reconstructed original sets like Jerry's apartment and Monk's Cafe, with Jerry's apartment updated to reflect the 11 years that had passed since the finale. This storyline finally gave fans the Seinfeld ending they had hoped for. "David previously refused to make a Seinfeld reunion, but he thought it would be funny to do it on Curb, because it would be the perfect way to do it, but not really do it."

xref.title: Solo Career Trajectory
xref.body: After The Smiths' breakup, Morrissey initially seemed poised to become a major solo star, benefiting from the cult following he amassed with his previous band. However, his solo career began to decline in the mid-1990s, as he struggled to produce consistent albums, moved to Los Angeles, refused interviews, and toured less frequently. "Although it got off to a promising start, Morris' solo career hit the skids in the mid 1990s."

xref.title: Steve Albini's Master Tapes Hostage Situation
xref.body: Producer Steve Albini had a deal stipulating no changes after his final mix. When the label wanted modifications to *In Utero*, he refused to hand over the master tapes, "essentially holding them hostage," until bassist Chris Novoselic convinced him to comply. "He even refused to hand over the master tapes for a while, essentially holding them hostage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Studio Problems at Cielo Drive
xref.body: While recording "The Downward Spiral" at 10,050 Cielo Drive, the former site of the Manson family murders, the studio equipment mysteriously and frequently broke down or refused to work. "But the equipment mysteriously, frequently broke down or refused to work."

xref.body: Ted Nugent was one of the musicians who publicly supported Donald Trump, distinguishing himself from many artists who refused to perform at Trump's events. "Outside of Kid Rock, Ted Nugent, three doors down and ace freely."

xref.title: TVT Records Contract Dispute
xref.body: After signing with TVT Records, the label's owner, Steve Gottlieb, disliked Trent's debut album "Pretty Hate Machine" for being too heavy and dark. When Steve demanded a more commercially palatable follow-up, Trent refused and sought release from his contract. TVT denied his request, putting him in "limbo for a couple of years" and forbidding him from recording or releasing new music, even allowing "Pretty Hate Machine" to go out of print. This forced Trent to record secretly under fake names. "But when Steve demanded that the follow up record be more commercially palatable, Trent not so respectfully declined and demanded that he be led out of his contract."

xref.title: Tom Wally's Unusual Meeting
xref.body: When Warner Brothers President Tom Wally wanted to meet Billy Talent, he refused to leave his New Jersey beach house. The band was flown to New Jersey, played a "s***ly little session" in a rented airplane hanger with unfamiliar gear, while Wally sat looking at the floor, preoccupied with his house. After the performance, he still wanted to sign them but only allowed them to eat on his patio during a family birthday, providing fried chicken and beer. "Tom Wally had, he wanted to see us. He was the president of Warner Brothers. And he didn't want to leave his beach house in New Jersey to come to the city. So they took us to New Jersey, rented an airplane hanger. We played the s***ly little session in front of him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Victims of Industry Sexism
xref.body: Despite their talent and championship by figures like David Bowie, Fanny's career was hindered by the "old boys club" in the music industry. They were not given due credit as musicians and songwriters, instead being pressured to conform to expectations of being "cute" and "sexy," which they refused. "Unfortunately, Fanny became a victim of the old boys club in the recorded music industry, and weren't given their dues as musicians and songwriters."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: History of Female Drummers

xref.title: Vision Impairment from Unchanged Glasses Prescription
xref.body: Due to his OCD, Joey was particular about his eyeglasses but refused to update his prescription, which consequently impaired his vision. "Joey was very particular about his glasses in his OCD way and refused to get his prescription updated. And consequently, his vision wasn't what it could have been."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: `SCTV` Topless Compromise
xref.body: When booked on the Canadian TV show `SCTV`, Wendy O'Williams refused to wear a top. A compromise was reached where a makeup artist painted her breasts black to conceal them on air. "When the Plasmatics were booked on the old Canadian TV show, SCTV, she refused to wear a top. The salvage, everything the compromise was to have the makeup artist paint her breasts black so you couldn't tell."
